newsitem.title: USA: Supreme Court halts execution of Virginia man.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court halts execution of Virginia man.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court halted the execution of Douglas MacArthur Buchanan Jr. just four hours before he was to die on Tuesday for the 1987 murders of his father, stepmother and two stepbrothers.
In its one-paragraph order, the court agreed to stay the execution until it decides whether to hear his appeal. A spokesman for the Virginia Attorney General's office declined to comment.

The order said that if the justices decided not to hear the appeal, the stay would end automatically and a new execution date would be set. If they agree to hear the case, the stay will be extended until a decision has been made.
Gerald Zerkin, one of Buchanan's lawyers, said he was happy with the decision and that his client "was pleased as well."

Officials at the Greensville Correctional Centre had been prepared to carry out the execution by lethal injection at 9 p.m. EDT. It would have been the third in the state this year and the 40th since executions resumed in the United States in 1977.

Buchanan, 29, was sentenced to die for the brutal 1987 murders of his father, Douglas MacArthur Buchanan Sr., his stepmother, Geraldine Buchanan, and stepbrothers Donnie, 10 and Joel, 13, which shocked the tiny mountain community of Naola.

Evidence showed that on the day of the killings the younger Buchanan and his wife, Christianne Marie, parked on the Blue Ridge Parkway a short walk from the family's mobile home and discussed the murders.

Buchanan shot his father in the back of the head and then between the eyes. He shot stepbrother Donnie, then fired two shots at Joel as he tried to flee. He then dragged the boys into a bedroom, where Joel was stabbed five times in the head as he tried to flee again.

He shot his stepmother with his father's handgun, stabbed her in the chest and slit her throat so severely she was nearly decapitated. Buchanan and his wife fled and were later arrested in New Mexico.
Christianne Buchanan is serving four life terms on four counts of being an accessory before the fact and encouraging her husband in the slayings.

Buchanan never denied the killings. An expert witness testified he suffered from an emotionally brutal upbringing and acted "under extreme mental or emotional disturbance" when he killed his family. But the jury and judge decided he acted with premeditation.
Buchanan did not petition Gov. George Allen for clemency but Allen, in a statement released before the Supreme Court acted, said "his guilt is clear" and that he did not intend to intervene.

The appeal to the Supreme Court contends Buchanan's jury was not given adequate instructions by the judge on mitigating circumstances during the penalty phase of the trial. It also argues the jury should have been allowed to hear more evidence about Buchanan's background as an abused child.
Experts in the case agreed he had been mistreated at the hands of his father and stepmother.
